lead: Diathermy means heating deep tissue on purpose without cutting the skin. A short-wave unit passes a radio-frequency current through the body at 27.12 MHz. A microwave unit beams 2450 MHz energy into tissue. An ultrasonic unit sends 0.8–1 MHz sound waves through a coupling gel. The tissue absorbs the energy and becomes warm. This relieves pain, relaxes muscle spasm and speeds repair in physiotherapy. Surgical diathermy uses the same radio-frequency idea to cut and coagulate, but that is a separate application, not therapy.
prereq: You need: basic AC circuits — frequency f in hertz, wavelength λ = c ÷ f with c the speed of light, and impedance — plus the idea that current needs a complete path.

blocks.text: A short-wave diathermy unit takes 50 Hz mains, rectifies it, and feeds an oscillator. The oscillator runs at 27.12 MHz. A power amplifier raises the signal to a useful output, commonly a few hundred watts at most. A matching network tunes the amplifier to the patient, because the body is not a fixed 50 ohm load. The output then reaches the applicator: two insulated plates, or a coil. In capacitive coupling the plates sit on either side of the limb, so the tissue between them is the dielectric (the material between the plates) and it heats. In inductive coupling a coil is placed near the body and its changing magnetic field induces small circulating currents, called eddy currents. Some units allow both.

Tissue heats by two losses. Dielectric loss: the alternating electric field makes polar water molecules rotate. Their collisions with neighbours turn field energy into heat. Resistive loss: ions in tissue drift with the field and collide. Both depend on frequency and on tissue composition. Muscle has more water and ions than fat, so it usually absorbs more short-wave energy.

The body is not heated by a travelling beam at this frequency. The free-space wavelength, about 11 m, is far longer than the limb, so the tissue sits in the near field between the plates or under the coil. Tissue absorbs relatively little of a 27.12 MHz field per centimetre, so the heating reaches deep muscle. As frequency rises, absorption per centimetre rises and the heating stays nearer the surface. 27.12 MHz is a reserved industrial–scientific–medical frequency, not any random short-wave radio channel. 13.56 MHz is also used.

Microwave diathermy uses 2450 MHz. A microwave oscillator, such as a magnetron, feeds a reflector applicator. The applicator directs a beam into the tissue, and the water in tissue absorbs it. The wavelength in air is about 12.2 cm, but tissue absorbs strongly, so useful heating is only a few centimetres deep. Keep the applicator at the stated distance. Do not treat over the eye or testis, where little tissue protects the organ. Microwaves are convenient for superficial joints and muscles.

Ultrasonic diathermy uses a piezoelectric transducer (a crystal that vibrates when driven by a voltage) at 0.8–1 MHz. The transducer converts electrical drive into mechanical vibration. A coupling gel removes air, because air reflects ultrasound. The beam enters tissue and is absorbed; the patient feels warmth. 1 MHz reaches several centimetres. 3 MHz is used for more superficial tissue. Bone and air interfaces absorb or reflect strongly, so avoid directing the beam across a bone edge or through air.

All three methods raise tissue temperature. On short-wave and microwave units the dial sets output power in watts and a timer sets the minutes. On an ultrasound unit the dial sets intensity, the power per square centimetre of the head, usually 0.1–3 W/cm²; total power is intensity times the effective radiating area (ERA) of the head, and pulsed mode, for example 20 % on, lowers the average heating. The operator starts low and asks the patient about warmth and pain. Skin sensation is the safety sensor; if it is impaired, the patient cannot warn of a burn.

Dose is not just a number on the dial. It is power in watts applied for a time in minutes, and it depends on the applicator, the body part and the patient's sensation. A physiotherapy session may last 10–20 minutes, but the setting is adjusted to a comfortable warmth. Burns can occur at high power, with poor coupling, with wrinkled towels or with a metal implant that concentrates the field.

Contraindications include metal implants in the field, pregnancy over the abdomen or pelvis, ischaemic tissue (poor blood supply), bleeding tissue and impaired sensation. A cardiac pacemaker or other electronic implant is also a reason to avoid short-wave and microwave diathermy, because the field can interfere with the device. Do not treat over the eye, testis or growing bone with microwave or ultrasound unless specifically trained.

Surgical diathermy, or electrosurgery, uses radio-frequency current for cutting and coagulation (clotting). A small active electrode creates high current density, so tissue vaporises and the cut seals small vessels. A large return plate spreads the current. It is not therapy and not the same as heating a joint. The same RF principle appears in cardiac ablation, where a catheter burns a small patch of heart muscle; see defibrillator protection and cardiac ablation.

figure.caption: The chain from 50 Hz mains to a 27.12 MHz field between two plates across the limb. The worked example gives λ = 11.06 m and T = 36.9 ns, so the limb sits in the near field and the field passes through fat into muscle; the ultrasound example gives 7.5 W, 2250 J and a 1.54 mm wavelength.

examples.question: A short-wave diathermy unit works at 27.12 MHz. Find the wavelength in air and the period of the wave.
steps: Given f = 27.12 MHz = 27.12 × 10⁶ Hz and c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

The 11 m wavelength is far bigger than the limb, so the tissue sits in the near field of the plates and is heated by the field directly. The depth comes from the low absorption per centimetre at this frequency; at 2450 MHz absorption is much higher and the heating stays within a few centimetres.
examples.answer: Wavelength λ = 11.06 m and period T = 36.9 ns.

examples.question: An ultrasound therapy head has an effective radiating area of 5 cm² and works at 1 MHz. It is set to 1.5 W/cm² continuous for 5 minutes. (a) Find the output power and the energy delivered. (b) Repeat for pulsed mode at a 20 % duty cycle with the same setting. (c) Find the wavelength in soft tissue, where sound travels at 1540 m/s.
steps: Continuous power P = intensity × ERA = 1.5 W/cm² × 5 cm² = 7.5 W.
Time t = 5 × 60 = 300 s, so energy E = P t = 7.5 W × 300 s = 2250 J.
Pulsed at 20 %: average intensity = 0.2 × 1.5 = 0.3 W/cm², average power = 0.3 × 5 = 1.5 W and energy = 1.5 × 300 = 450 J, one fifth of the continuous dose.
Wavelength in tissue λ = v ÷ f = 1540 m/s ÷ (1 × 10⁶ Hz) = 1.54 × 10⁻³ m = 1.54 mm.
Compare: the short-wave field has an 11 m wavelength, the ultrasound beam 1.54 mm. The short wavelength is why ultrasound forms a narrow beam that can be aimed, and why bone edges reflect it.
examples.answer: Continuous: 7.5 W and 2250 J; pulsed at 20 %: 1.5 W average and 450 J; wavelength in tissue 1.54 mm.

traps: Do not write that higher frequency always means deeper heating. For electromagnetic diathermy it is the opposite: 2450 MHz microwaves heat only a few centimetres, while 27.12 MHz short waves heat deeper.
Do not call 27.12 MHz just a convenient short-wave radio band. It is a reserved industrial–scientific–medical (ISM) frequency; 13.56 MHz is another.
Do not treat diathermy and surgical diathermy as the same. Therapeutic diathermy warms tissue; electrosurgery cuts and coagulates with concentrated RF current.
Do not say the dose is set by power alone. It is power, or for ultrasound intensity in W/cm², applied for a time, and it also depends on coupling, the applicator and the patient's sensation.
Do not write that 3 MHz ultrasound penetrates deeper than 1 MHz. Absorption rises with frequency, so 3 MHz heats more superficially.

quiz.q: State the standard frequency and two applicator arrangements for short-wave diathermy.
quiz.a: 27.12 MHz; insulated capacitive plates or an inductive coil.
Metal implants in the field and pregnancy over the abdomen or pelvis; also ischaemic or bleeding tissue.

quiz.q: Why is a matching network needed between the amplifier and the applicator plates?
quiz.a: The patient's impedance changes with body part and coupling. The network tunes the output to that impedance, so power transfers efficiently and the amplifier is not damaged by a mismatch.

quiz.q: Why does muscle usually heat more than fat in short-wave diathermy?
quiz.a: Muscle has more water and ions, so both dielectric loss and resistive loss are larger. Fat has less polar water and lower conductivity, so it absorbs less.

quiz.q: A microwave diathermy unit runs at 2450 MHz. Find the wavelength in air.
A short-wave unit delivers 200 W for 10 minutes. Find the energy in joules.
Why does 1 MHz ultrasound reach deeper than 3 MHz ultrasound?
quiz.a: Absorption rises with frequency. At 3 MHz, the energy is absorbed in the first centimetres, so less reaches deep tissue. At 1 MHz, absorption per centimetre is lower, so the beam penetrates further.

quiz.q: A patient with a hip implant needs deep heating of the thigh. Why is short-wave diathermy risky, and what should be done?
quiz.a: Metal conducts, so it concentrates the field and the current around it and the tissue next to the implant can burn while the skin feels only mild warmth. Do not use short-wave or microwave diathermy over or near the implant; choose a treatment that keeps the implant well outside the field, or another method, following the local safety rules.

beyond: Not for the exam. Microwave ablation and radio-frequency ablation now destroy tumours and faulty heart tissue using the same heating idea, with imaging guidance. High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) uses focused ultrasound to heat a small volume while sparing skin. Wearable and phased-array applicators are research areas for controlled deep heating. Search terms: microwave ablation, RF ablation, HIFU, specific absorption rate (SAR), diathermy safety.
